words.d: a short movie in a game where the player doesn't control anything
a staged story moment that happens while the player keeps control
voice over: recorded lines spoken by actors
a cheap test recording used only to check timing
a short voice reaction, like "Got it!" or a battle cry
first-time user experience: the player's first minutes in the game

cards.text: Cutscenes look great, but many players skip them. **Before making one, ask: could this moment happen in gameplay instead?**
A cutscene moves the story, creates spectacle and shows characters. But many have been too long, pointless or boring, so players learned to skip them.
The chapter's title is the warning: "No one's gonna watch 'em anyway." Design so the game makes sense even if nobody watches. Viewers get a bonus.
Mobile players open the app to play. Every second of unskippable movie in the first minutes loses players. Turn the beat into a level goal, a task like "fix the stairs", or one speech bubble.
It's always better to have the player do than watch.

check.q: What should you ask before making a cutscene?
options: Could this happen in gameplay instead?
check.why: Playing beats watching. Use cutscenes only for what play can't do.

cards.text: Cutscenes range from Hollywood-style film to fully playable moments. **Pick the type that fits your style, budget and schedule.**

- **FMV:** live-action film with real actors
- **Animated:** hand-drawn or stop-motion
- **Flash:** still images with simple movement
- **Prerendered:** high-quality CG
- **Puppet show:** game models with a movie camera
- **Scripted event:** the player keeps control
Since Half-Life and Call of Duty, scripted events became the favourite way to tell stories, because play never stops.
**Groundhog Day problem:** a scene that replays every time you retry makes players furious. Show it once, then skip it automatically on retries.
Film, Frames, Flash, Fancy render, Puppets, Play: from most Hollywood to most game.

check.q: What is the Groundhog Day problem?
options: A scene replays every time the player retries
check.why: Repeating the same scene after every failure frustrates players.

cards.text: A scripted event the player doesn't see is wasted money. **Stage it like a theme-park ride: control where they look.**

- Start the event only when the player is facing it.
- Shape the level so walls and paths frame the view.
- If the camera moves, start from the player's own view.
- Always show cause and effect.
Pull a lever, then the camera shows which door opens. Players should never wonder what their action did.
On mobile, dim the screen except the thing to tap, so the player can't miss it. When a new area unlocks, pan the camera across it.
If a tree falls in a scripted event and the player was looking at the minimap, it didn't happen.

check.q: Why start a scripted event only when the player faces it?
check.why: An event nobody sees is wasted work.

lessons.title: Plan the script: outline, scenes, play

cards.text: Game writers are writing professionals. The first steps of a script are **outline, break it into scenes, and decide what's played versus watched.**

- **Outline:** know the beginning, middle and end.
- **Scenes:** list who appears and where. This drives art and staging.
- **Order:** start with a bang. A flashback can open on the best action.
Save cutscenes for big moments the engine can't play, like **kissing and explosions**. If the player could perform the moment, don't film it.
Even a 5-day event needs a mini outline: open with the most dramatic moment, and put the finale on the last day.

check.q: What does Rogers say cutscenes are best for?
options: Big moments the engine can't play, like kissing and explosions
check.why: Everything else should be played, not watched.

lessons.title: Write short, then read it aloud

cards.text: Be brief. Show with action more than words. **Then read every line out loud**, because lines that look fine on paper often sound clumsy.

- Use the standard screenplay format, like every other entertainment professional.
- Let the script rest a day or two, then rewrite.
- Ask someone else to read it, and don't hover while they read.
Harrison Ford famously told George Lucas that Star Wars dialogue could be typed but not said.
In mobile speech bubbles, the rules apply double: short, funny, one idea per bubble.
Brevity is the soul of wit, and of speech bubbles.

options: Lines that look fine can sound clumsy when spoken
check.why: Spoken lines reveal problems that reading hides.

cards.text: Voice actors read **exactly what's written**. Prepare a clean spreadsheet: one line per row, a file name and notes on how to say it.
Write sounds the way you want them performed. A short "Arg!" and a long "Aaaargh!" are completely different. Comic books are great for sound words like POW and AIIEEE.
Hit and death sounds need separate takes: falling off a cliff, getting shot, getting burned, plus extra versions.
Most casual games skip full voice acting because of cost, languages and download size. They use **barks** (short reactions), gibberish voices or an announcer, like Candy Crush's "Sweet!".
Arg is a pirate. Aaaargh is a funeral.

check.why: The spelling tells the actor how long and how intense the sound is.

cards.text: Record a cheap **temp track** to check timing, then hire **professional actors** through a **voice director**.
Team members read the lines to measure length. Never animate lip sync to a temp track: the real performance will be different.
The voice director casts the actors, books the studio and directs the session. Describe characters clearly. You can even name a famous actor you imagine.
The writer must be in the room, because lines change constantly. Let actors improvise: you get more material, and they'll want to work with you again.

check.q: What is a temp track for?
check.why: Real actors perform differently, so temp audio is only for timing.

lessons.title: The skip button is not optional

cards.text: On mobile, story is seasoning. **Every story moment must be skippable**, short, and ideally playable.

- Allow skipping from the first frame.
- Remember what the player has seen, and never replay it on a retry.
- Offer a recap or story log for people who skipped.
A rough guideline: keep story beats **under about 10 seconds** or **2–3 bubbles** before the player gets control back.
Turn explanation into a tap: the player opens the letter, places the first sofa, fires the first cannon. Watch skip rates and drop-off right after each story beat.

check.q: How long should a mobile story beat usually be?
options: As long as the writer wants
check.why: Players came to play. Short beats keep the story without losing them.

cards.text: Casual games tell stories through **short character bubbles** between levels, and give **every event a mini-story**.
Homescapes (with Austin the butler) and Merge Mansion use quick bubbles between tasks. Choices and Episode make dialogue the core loop, with choices as the gameplay.
A villain arrives, a festival needs saving, a new chapter of a mystery opens. The story gives players a reason to care about this week's event goal.
Season updates work like TV seasons: a teaser, weekly beats and a finale. The guided first level is itself a scripted event: staged, focused, clear, and no longer than it must be.

check.q: Why give a LiveOps event a mini-story?
options: It gives players a reason to care about the event goal
check.why: Story turns "collect 500 tokens" into a goal that means something.

lessons.title: Trailers and ads are cutscenes too

cards.text: On mobile, big cinematic movies mostly live in **marketing**. Snack-size story inside the game, feast-size trailers outside it.
Supercell is famous for animated Clash trailers and shorts that build its characters. Clash of Clans even had a 2015 Super Bowl ad starring Liam Neeson.
An ad is a tiny cutscene: hook in the first 1–3 seconds, clear cause and effect, and readable with the sound off.
Show what players will actually play. Regulators like the UK's ad watchdog have ruled against game ads that showed gameplay not in the game.
Snack-size story, feast-size trailer.

check.q: Where does big cinematic content mostly live for mobile games?
check.why: Inside the game, story stays short. Big cinema builds the brand in marketing.
